title: The Happening
full_review:
With its shifting clouds and creepy music, the opening credit sequence of "The Happening" (Fox) bodes well for a return to form for director M. Night Shyamalan, whose most recent films, though atmospheric, have failed to match the overall quality of his breakout hit, "The Sixth Sense."

Instead, this film emerges as an intriguing if only sporadically scary thriller, albeit with a well-intended though rather obvious social message.

In the opening scene, strange happenings are afoot in New York's Central Park, as afternoon strollers are suddenly frozen in time, and a young lady placidly reading on a bench is suddenly compelled to take out her hairpin and stab herself in the neck. A few blocks away, construction workers begin hurling themselves off a building, hitting the ground with dreadful thuds. What's going on?

Cut to a Philadelphia high school, where science teacher Elliot Moore (Mark Wahlberg) is interrupted in his discourse on the mysterious disappearance of the world's honeybees by the principal, who tells her staff to send the students home.

With his emotionally fragile (actually, downright kooky) therapist wife Alma (Zooey Deschanel) -- consumed with guilt over a mild flirtation with a male colleague -- his best friend, Julian (John Leguizamo), and Julian's young daughter, Jess (Ashlyn Sanchez), they join the masses fleeing town by train. Once on their way, the passengers hear of another cataclysmic event back home. Eventually, the passengers are made to disembark in tiny Filbert, Pa.

Before long, even this sleepy burg begins to show signs of the epidemic, which as we now realize, causes those infected to kill themselves. Is this a terrorist attack as the few remaining newscasts are reporting? Or, as science teacher Elliot surmises, might it have something to do with the plants and trees, which tremble and sway in the wind whenever anything bad is about to happen?

Before long, Julian is frantic to find his wife, with whom he's lost contact, and he takes off for Princeton, N.J., to find her, leaving little Jess in the care of Elliot and Alma.

Wahlberg gives his most emotionally nuanced performance to date, but it's Broadway's Betty Buckley who steals the film as a crazed old lady who gives the three shelter.

Shyamalan's direction per se is as skillful as ever, and graphic violence is relatively restrained, despite the film's vaunted R-rating (his first). But much of the illogical character motivation, an overall sense of contrivance, stilted dialogue and lame attempts at humor undermine the whole.

The film's overriding theme is, as noted, an admirable one, and the gradual healing of Elliot and Alma's troubled marriage is touchingly conveyed.

But perhaps it's time to see what the talented Shyamalan might achieve if he branched out to another genre.

The film contains some very brief but grisly images of murder, mayhem and death, brief profanity and a couple of crude words, multiple but mostly nongraphic suicides, and a fleeting sexual reference. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
